## P2-Q1

**Запрос.** Explain in prose first, do not start with a table. nikic/php-parser
versus PHP token_get_all for building a static source inventory: which language
constructs require a full AST (group use statements, aliases, attributes,
fully-qualified names in strings, class names in config arrays) and which a
tokenizer cannot recover. Official php-parser documentation and PHP tokenizer
docs. Name primary-source URLs.

**Статус.** success

**Смысловые утверждения (дословно по содержанию ответа).**

For a static source inventory, use nikic/php-parser when the inventory must be
semantically trustworthy: declarations, inheritance, trait use, attributes,
imports and aliases, references, and canonical fully qualified class names. Use
token_get_all() only for a deliberately shallow, lexical pass.

PHP’s official documentation describes token_get_all() as splitting source into
tokens using the Zend lexical scanner; its output is token IDs/text/line numbers
plus one-character punctuation tokens—not a parsed syntax tree.

nikic/php-parser parses source into an AST, exposes location information,
supports traversal, and provides namespace-name resolution. Its NameResolver uses
the current namespace, import table, and symbol kind to resolve names to fully
qualified forms where PHP’s static rules permit that.

Strictly speaking, no valid PHP syntax is information-theoretically hidden from
token_get_all(). The raw token stream contains the source spelling. With enough
code, you can build a parser, track brace depth, implement namespace/import
scope, and perform PHP name resolution. But that implementation is effectively a
partial compiler front end. It will tend to fail on: multiple namespace
declarations; bracketed namespace syntax; imports aliased by as; group imports
with nested per-item aliases; use in different grammatical positions (namespace
import vs trait composition vs closure capture); attributes; constructor property
promotion; union/intersection types; anonymous classes.

Even TOKEN_PARSE does not solve this. The PHP manual says it affects recognition
of reserved words in context; it still returns a flat token stream.

Neither AST nor tokens can fully resolve values constructed dynamically:
reflection, concatenation, variables, environment values, container bindings,
class_alias(), code generation, or Laravel’s convention-driven discovery. Those
should be explicit inventory categories such as static, convention-derived, and
dynamic/unresolved.

PHP-Parser documents that an unqualified function or constant reference inside a
namespace may fall back to the global namespace at runtime and cannot be fully
resolved from static context alone.

**Первичные источники.**

- https://www.php.net/manual/en/function.token-get-all.php
- https://www.php.net/manual/en/book.tokenizer.php
- https://github.com/nikic/PHP-Parser
- https://github.com/nikic/PHP-Parser/blob/master/doc/component/Name_resolution.markdown

## P2-Q2

**Запрос.** Explain in prose first, do not start with a table. In a PHP monorepo,
how do teams distinguish three dependency graphs: Composer declared require, PHP
namespace imports from use statements, and runtime container or service-provider
bindings. What discrepancy does each pair reveal, especially hidden string-based
class coupling. Practices from Symfony Flex, Laravel package discovery, and
modular monolith literature. Name primary-source URLs.

**Статус.** success

**Смысловые утверждения.**

Teams usually model these as three different projections of coupling, not as
competing dependency definitions:

- Composer graph answers: which deployable packages are declared to be available.
- PHP source graph answers: which namespaces/classes this code statically refers to.
- Runtime composition graph answers: which abstractions are actually wired to
  which implementations when the application boots.

They should not be expected to match edge-for-edge. A clean modular monolith
deliberately has differences. The important thing is to make every difference
explainable—and to treat unexplained differences as architectural debt.

Composer `require` is the strongest statement of declared package-level intent,
never proof that a package is actually used. A declared dependency may be unused;
a package can arrive transitively; `autoload.files`, facades, reflection,
configuration, and Laravel discovery can introduce behavior the require graph
does not express.

A robust source analyzer must inspect more than `use`: fully qualified names,
type declarations, attributes, inheritance, traits, static calls and `::class`,
PHPDoc types if they affect analysis, function/const imports, and framework
artifacts (listeners, commands, jobs, policies).

The runtime graph includes bind/singleton/scoped/instance/bindIf, contextual
bindings, aliases, tags, extenders, provider registration order,
environment-conditional registrations, factory closures, and event/route/command
registrations. It is often better modeled as: consumer → requested abstraction →
provider declaration → selected implementation.

Hidden string-based coupling: `app('…')`, `make($className)`, `config('…')`,
`Event::listen('name', …)`, morph maps, raw FQCN strings, facade accessors,
package `extra` metadata that triggers discovery. The right response is not
necessarily to ban strings; it is to make their semantics typed, centralized,
and testable.

Symfony Flex demonstrates that the Composer graph and the runtime/configuration
graph are distinct: `composer require` may apply a recipe that changes config,
env, bundles, routes; `symfony.lock` records those side effects. Laravel package
discovery makes the Composer-to-runtime bridge direct via `extra.laravel`
providers/facades and `dont-discover`.

A module may consume another module only through an exported PHP contract, an
application-level event/message contract, or a deliberately documented runtime
token. Composition-root bindings that point a contract at an infrastructure
adapter are an expected difference, not a violation.

**Первичные источники.**

- https://getcomposer.org/doc/04-schema.md
- https://getcomposer.org/doc/01-basic-usage.md
- https://symfony.com/doc/current/setup.html
- https://github.com/symfony/flex
- https://laravel.com/docs/12.x/packages
- https://laravel.com/docs/12.x/container
- https://laravel.com/docs/12.x/providers
